The first thing that draws the eye to [b][i]Ori and the Blind Forest[/i][/b] is its beautiful art, and indeed playing this game is a feast for the senses, a 10 out of 10 on presentation alone. All the environments are gorgeously contructed and filled with luscious vibrant colours, the soundtrack is truly amazing and evocative, and the character animation is so fluid that controlling little Ori feels like a joy. All these elements combine to tell a simple but surprisingly emotional story that's reminiscent of early Ghibli movies, instilling a sense of awe for nature and having some earnestly moving moments. 

When it comes to platforming the thing I appreciate the most is having a free sense of movement when controlling my character, and [b][i]Ori and the Blind Forest[/i][/b] more than delivers on that front. While it may not seem so at first, once you've unlocked enough abilities Ori can freely double jump, climb walls, air glide, propel herself through enemy projectiles, and just generally cavort though the air like a magic acrobat, with the controls being so responsive that navigating though levels feels both very entertaining and challenging. (And I'm not kidding about the challenging part, it really does get harder later on so be warned.) Plus there are enough secret nooks and crannies, locked paths, and three kinds of collectibles/upgrades to find, to make exploring the entirety of a map feel suitably metroidvania-y and keep you occupied.

As for the combat, the game mixes up things a little: instead of your own character spinning around stunning enemies, you attack through your little fairy companion. What this basically boils down to is smashing the attack button while trying to dodge enemy attacks at the same time, so you do need a minimum of effort to win fights. There are also special attacks you can unlock, and there's a decent enough variety of enemies, although at points they cluster so close together and respawn so quickly that walking around and backtracking can be a bit of a chore. I also wish it wasn't so easy to die, because no matter how many health upgrades you have getting hit 3 times in a row always kills you, which I found super frustrating.

But the thing that's actually unique to this game is the checkpoint mechanic, where instead of having automatic savepoints you have to manually spend some energy and create one yourself. This can lead to interesting tactics, like choosing to keep your energy for special attacks and risk longer journeys, or sacrificing your energy for the sake of frequent checkpoints and health regeneration. And even though saving after every difficult sequence soon becomes a matter of habit, I definitely had a few face-palming moments when I realised just how long it had been since my last save, so it's another aspect to keep track of.

I honestly can't think of any complaints about the game, except maybe that I wish there was more of it! I could have easily and happily invested 20 and more hours in the game, but the story wraps up at around 8 or 9. Yet despite the low number it feels like a complete and satisfying game, and it's hard to begrudge the devs for the short playtime when the things you [i]do[/i] get to experience were so lovingly made. (And to be fair there are also quite a few achievements to hunt for although I'm not gonna lie, some were way too masochistic for me. Beating the entire game with one life on perma-death? No thanks!)

In any case, [b][i]Ori and the Blind Forest[/i][/b] is one of the best in its genre (in my opinion second only to Rayman Legends) and definitely worth a play if you like those kind of games.

Graphically Ori and the Blind Forest is phenomenal. Even after multiple years the game doesn't show any signs of aging. It still looks very impressive.

I just finished Ori and the Blind Forest.  And as always, it's time for a game review.

Ultimately, Ori and the Blind Forest is absolutely worth the full price.  So go out there and play this one!

Ori and the Blind Forest is that type of game that manages to struck me in awe.

It starts as simple hit and jump platformer and slowly becomes more and more difficult as we go. Along the journey, Ori gets power ups as the part of the story progression and the designers cleverly incorporate everything we learn to progress. Unlike normal platformers though, Ori includes some puzzles that requires players to carefully execute the movement, so could be source of frustration as sometimes you die more to level hazards (i.e spikes) than the enemies around the map.

And needless to say the graphic, level design and soundtrack are too beautiful for its own good. I can confidently say this is on par with Trine series, and Trine series are absolutely my favorite when it comes to graphic/level design for platformer games.

The only downside I can assess for Ori is its mediocre boss fight. It's really forgettable and sometimes I wonder did I really fight a boss? Felt like I was fighting a normal creep. Even a supposedly difficult [spoiler]final boss was no more than a quick jumping, running and reacting to hazardous environment.[/spoiler]

Please remember to use your controller to play the game as it is more enjoyable than smashing your keyboard's buttons because some levels require precise timing and movement.

If you're a completionist you'll have plenty of things to do as Ori has many hidden side quests and achievements. Personally I can't be bothered though but it's nice to have those things to do.

As it stands, I can fully recommend this game. Don't forget to pick up its soundtracks as well it's often on sale and you won't regret it.

It is about time I reviewed this game. 
With a classic pros and cons, of course,

PROS:

Ori has a great story, which wouldn't feel out of place in a Dinsey movie. The animations feel quite fluid, and Ori seems to respond to his environment. For example, when standing next to a cliff or a steep drop, Ori will stick out his arms and peer over the edge, with a mixture of fear and curiocity. In other words, Ori seems very much alive. The various enemies you encounter in this game are also smoothly animated, but they don't have the kind of dynamic feel Ori does. Some items in the environment also kinda seem to react to Ori.

Do not fear, though, this eye candy and storyline stuff is indeed built on some gameplay mechanics. Ori is, in fact, solidly inside the 2d action adventure puzzle platformer box. (which could also be called a Metroidvania, but that title doesn't really describe the genre, does it?). Ori and the Blind Forest revolves almost entirely about completing an area, to gain an ability or item to progress to the next area. Areas mostly consist of a combination of platforming and puzzle solving.

As far as those abilities themselves go... well, there are quite a few of them. Ori features the standard move set , including things like, wall jumping, gliding, dashing, and triple jumping, in addition to a feature unique to the game, called bash. All these abilities work to accomplish the goal of keeping Ori airborn for extended periods of time. Often platforming in Ori will be about getting up to somewhere, or down from somewhere. You do not do very much platforming horizontally. 

When I say that you do a lot of platforming, you should imagine yourself dying, and then dying, and then dying, and then dying, and then dying again, and then finally, after what feels like the 80th attempt, you make it. But dying in Ori, as long as you manage your spawn points, isn't all that bad. Respawns happen instantly, and as far as checkpoints go, you can place them on any safe stable ground, but you have to remember to do so yourself, and manage the energy it takes to make them. 

CONS:

And now we have come to the sad part of this review.
I have outlined above, a sample of the variety of movement options you have, but toward the end of the game your movement options get quite numerous. This works both for and against the game. It means puzzles and platforming sections can be fairly complex and challenging, but it can also make platforming quite an exercise in coordination and timing. Furthermore, the key bindings cannot be easily changed, making certain sequences kinda difficult. For example, bash, attack, and jump, are all controlled by the same finger on the controller, meaning you have to move your thumb around alot. This might have been intentional to make the game challenging, who knows. After playing Hollow Knight, where I have my controls carefully configured for efficiency, it felt clumsy. 

A slight problem I had on my absolutely mediocre laptop (if you want details on my PC, be content with this one snippet of information: Intel HD 520 mobile) is input lag, until I turned town my resolution. But that likely won't happen if you have a better computer. 

The other problem with this game was that the main story only lasts about 10 hours. While I felt accomplished when I finished it, but I didn't really feel like exploring more of the world. The game kinda lost its momentum. In other words, I didn't find the exploration aspect very strong, and there's no denying I play games almost primarily for that feeling of discovery. So the drive of this game is platforming and the story. 

Something I think could have been developed more in Ori (though it couldn't, because the devs ran out of buttons on the controller) is combat. You basically spam the attack button. No need to aim, or any of that complicated stuff. You can use the stamp, dash, and explosion attacks, but since Ori's movement is more fluid than precise I often found myself messing up, and basically dying to enemies annoyingly often. 

PARTING WORDS

Overall, this game was really fun, and if you want a story driven action adventure puzzle platformer, this might be your thing. 

Thanks for giving this a read,

Ori and the Blind Forest magically uplifts its gorgeous interconnected wooded world of majestic flora and hostile fauna through a viscerally melancholic narrative that elevates this sublime Metroidvania high above Nibel's leafy canopies. 

WHAT I LIKED:
+ Pixar's helium-fuelled 'Up' is infamous for its emotionally affecting initial ten minutes. Well, Moon Studios attempt to match that saddening experience through its prologue of Ori's upbringing with Naru. You. Will. Cry. If no tears are shed, the eyes will undoubtedly be moist as the player unexpectedly welcomes the sorrowful tone beneath the beautiful art direction that truly powers the narrative of Ori's journey. A cataclysmic event results in the forest withering into decay, with Ori tasked in reviving the Spirit Tree by recovering the forest's light. There's death. There's destruction. But much like the Circle of Life, a concept Moon Studios was heavily influenced by, there's life. And the Blind Forest wholesomely attests to this concept through a visually stunning and emotional story that is just as important as the gameplay on offer.
+ Nibel has a life of its own. The rural world of Nibel, ranging from the serene marshlands of Thornfelt Swamp to the blustery Ghibli-inspired Valley of the Wind, has a plethora of characteristics that compliment the traditional aspects of a Metroidvania. Exploration is vital, with Ori equipped with a sprawling interconnected map that allows the player to become accustomed to the local geography as well as seek out nearby secrets. Locating Spirit Wells to regain life and energy as well as indicating fast travel points. It may seem beautifully daunting initially, but once the player explores Nibel and head out to obtain each of the three elements, the world gradually ingrains itself into the mind. It is absurdly difficult to sublimely transition between areas and still make the change look natural, however Moon Studios did that with an abundance of confidence, truly granting Nibel the life it requires.
+ Jumping between branches, diving into cold waters and moving rocks to unlock ancient doors are all traditional aspects to the Metroidvania genre. Blind Forest certainly uses the floral environment to generate challenges, both from a combat and platforming perspective, however the sole standout that differentiates this game from others within the saturated genre is the use of "Soul Links". Using Ori's energy to create, these energy-infused beams of light serve as checkpoints throughout the game. The difficulty is implemented by the low abundance of energy crystals needed to allow Ori to create these "Soul Links", therefore invoking a strategy as to where and when the player should create these checkpoints. The platforming is tough, so activating a "Soul Link" after completing a tricky area would be advisable, as the player is more than likely to accidentally jump at the wrong time and allow Ori to get impaled by a thorn...
+ Ori starts off as a fragile guardian spirit, but will soon evolve into a speedy, combative, free-running beast through the use of an ability tree system. Slaying enemies, destroying certain flora and locating those valuable spirit containers will grant Ori the opportunity to gain new skills based on three distinct categories. Every single skill is deemed useful, either for traversal or combat enhancements, inciting the player to choose wisely before venturing further into the dangers that Nibel succinctly hides away. 
+ Nibel is brought to life through an ornate art direction that can only be surmised in one word: Beguiling. There's no other way to describe Blind Forest. The creative team at Moon Studios have produced one of the most gorgeous gaming experiences ever, often surpassing the vast majority of AAA titles. From the 3D animated character models populating the vibrant water-coloured backdrops to the softly epic score that is teeming with life. There is not a single line, colour or detail out of place!
+ Ori's journey to save Nibel is a short quest. Fortunately it never outstays it welcome, with a plethora of collectibles to be found and an array of difficulties added in the Definitive Edition which all increase the replay value. The "One Life" difficulty is, to be bluntly, absurd mostly due to the only complaint that could be found...

WHAT I DISLIKED:
- ...the escape sequences. Ori never really faces off against a boss, mostly due to the focus on precise platforming rather than aggressive combat. Instead, after each element is obtained, Ori must flee from a threat that seeks to end him. This could be rapidly rising waters with the player tasked in ascending a tower before Ori drowns, or a ferocious owl swooping in every five seconds. These sequences generate an artificial difficulty that pushes Ori's newfound abilities to generate tension and pressure, more so than having the player moving around normally. The problem is with the absurd "trial and error" approach and the lack of checkpoints that ultimately incites repetition in order for the player to learn the traps and obstacles before moving on. Repetition is the antithesis of fun. Whilst the tension is ramped up, the change in pace is not welcomed and provokes several unnecessary rage-inducing moments in what is otherwise a near-perfect game.

VERDICT:
